name: Kondo
subcategory: personal CRM for your professional network
tagline: A personal CRM layer for keeping track of the people in your professional network and actually following up.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The data model here is embarrassingly simple: people, notes, tags, last contacted, next nudge. An agent will hand you a working local version of that in an afternoon and it will genuinely work, because the hard part of relationship tracking is discipline, not software. What you cannot one-shot is the plumbing that makes it feel effortless: pulling your network in automatically, sitting inside the interface where the conversations actually happen, and noticing when someone changes jobs. That plumbing means a browser extension against a platform that actively dislikes browser extensions, which is a project, not a session. Build the local version, accept that you will paste and import by hand, and see if you still open it in three weeks.
coreLoopDIY: A local single-user contact log where you import a CSV of your network, tag people, write notes after each conversation, and get a queue of who is overdue for a follow-up.
requirements: A CSV export of your connections from whatever network you care about
whatYouLose: No in-context UI where you actually talk to people, so logging is a separate deliberate act
No automatic enrichment: job changes, new titles and profile updates never appear unless you type them
No message or inbox sync, so conversation history lives in the other app and your notes drift out of date
No mobile client and no sync, so it is a desktop-only habit
Nobody maintaining the scraping layer when the platform changes its markup next quarter
moatNotes: The moat is not the CRM, it is living inside someone else's product without breaking, which is ongoing maintenance work rather than a clever idea.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a personal CRM you have to remember to open is a personal CRM you stop opening. The paid product's whole pitch is proximity: it is already there when you are talking to the person, so the note costs you two seconds instead of a context switch. That proximity is bought with extension engineering and constant repair against a hostile host, which is exactly the kind of unglamorous recurring cost people happily rent instead of own. Also, your DIY version's contact list is a snapshot from the day you exported it, and reality keeps moving.
notes: The database schema is a fifteen minute job; the follow-through is the product, and no code fixes that.
prompt:
Build a local single-user personal CRM. Ship it as one Next.js 15 app (App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind) with SQLite via better-sqlite3 and Drizzle. No auth, no accounts, no cloud, no telemetry. It runs on localhost and stores everything in ./data/crm.db.

Data model:
- person: id, full_name, headline, company, profile_url, email, tags (many-to-many), cadence_days (nullable), last_contacted_at (nullable), created_at, archived (bool)
- note: id, person_id, body (markdown), happened_on (date), created_at
- tag: id, name, color

Features, in scope:
1. CSV import at /import. Accept a connections-style export with First Name, Last Name, Company, Position, URL, Email Address columns. Show a mapping preview before writing. Dedupe on profile_url, then on email, then on exact name. Never create duplicates on re-import; update blank fields only.
2. People list with instant client-side fuzzy search, tag filter chips, and sort by overdue.
3. Person detail page: inline-editable fields, tag editor, reverse-chronological notes, and a "log a conversation" box that appends a note and sets last_contacted_at to today in one action.
4. A /queue page: everyone whose last_contacted_at plus cadence_days is in the past or null-cadence-and-never-contacted, sorted by most overdue. Each row has snooze 7 days and "logged it" buttons.
5. Quick add: a single text field that parses "Name, Company" and creates a person in one keystroke path.
6. Export everything to JSON and CSV from a /settings page. This is the escape hatch, make it work.

Explicitly out of scope: browser extensions, scraping any website, message or inbox sync, contact enrichment, email sending, multi-user, sharing, mobile app, background jobs.

Use a single seed script that inserts ten fake people so the UI is not empty on first run. Keep any config in .env.local read via process.env; there are no secrets needed, so do not invent any. Ship a README with exactly the commands to install, seed, and run.

Optimize for keyboard speed over visual polish: cmd-k palette that jumps to a person or opens quick add, and Enter to submit every form.
